title: What Should I Do Before Trying for a Baby?
seoTitle: What to do before trying for a baby
description: A short preconception checklist: folic acid, medicines, vaccines, chronic conditions, tobacco and alcohol, and partner health—without a blanket test stack.
primaryQuestion: What should I do before trying for a baby?
directAnswer: Before trying for a baby, review your medicines, vaccination records, chronic conditions, tobacco and alcohol use, and partner health with a clinician—without stopping prescriptions on your own. India's National Health Mission advises 400 mcg folic acid tablets daily through the preconception period and first trimester; WHO also supports 400 μg daily across the trying-to-conceive window into week 12. The aim is safer next steps for your history, not a universal fertility scan or supplement stack.

sections.heading: What a preconception review is for
paragraphs: A preconception visit is a planned conversation before a positive test—or as soon as you decide pregnancy is a near-term goal. It covers cycle patterns, previous pregnancies, long-term conditions, operations, infections, mental health and family history from both sides when relevant. Dr. Charmi Shah uses that history to decide what is useful for you, rather than copying a chemist aisle list or a friend's test package.

You do not need perfect health before conception. Earlier review is especially helpful if you take regular medicines, live with diabetes, thyroid disease, hypertension or epilepsy, have had pregnancy complications, or know of an inherited condition in either family. If trying has already begun, the same checklist still organises what to bring and what to ask.

sections.heading: A short prioritised action checklist
paragraphs: Folic acid: under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, India's National Health Mission advises reproductive-age women to take 400 mcg folic acid tablets daily in the preconception period and up to the first trimester. WHO guidance aligns on 400 μg daily while you are trying and through 12 weeks of gestation. Detail on higher prescribed amounts and label checks sits in our folic acid before pregnancy guide.

Current medicines: list every prescription, over-the-counter product, herbal remedy and supplement, with photos of labels if names are unclear. UK NHS planning advice is clear—do not stop any prescribed medicine until you have talked to your GP or specialist. Abrupt stops can create more risk than a planned change under supervision.

Vaccine records: bring what you have, especially rubella/MMR status. NHS guidance recommends the MMR vaccine before pregnancy if you have not already had it, because rubella in pregnancy can harm the baby. Ask which vaccines or blood checks apply to you and when; eligibility follows local guidance and your history.

Chronic conditions: if you live with diabetes, thyroid disease, hypertension, epilepsy or another long-term condition, ask how stable care should look before conception and who will lead monitoring once pregnant. NHS advice is to speak to a GP when planning pregnancy with these conditions or with sickle cell disease or HIV.
Tobacco and alcohol: stop smoking and do not drink alcohol while trying and in pregnancy—NHS planning pages list both as core preparation steps, with support available if you need help quitting.

Partner considerations: where sperm is involved, ask about the partner's medicines, smoking, alcohol, workplace exposures and any previous fertility or semen evaluation. Preconception care should not place the entire burden on one person.

sections.heading: What you do not need by default
paragraphs: Most couples do not need a blanket fertility scan package, anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) testing, a broad hormone panel or a stacked “prenatal booster” shelf before the first conversation. Those tools answer specific clinical questions; ordering them from social media advice often adds cost and anxiety without changing decisions.

Leave with a short written plan: which medicines stay, change or need specialist input; which vaccinations or tests are timed and when; what lifestyle changes you are attempting first; and whom to contact after a positive pregnancy test. If cycles are irregular, pelvic pain is significant, or there is a known reproductive condition, ask whether earlier fertility discussion is warranted rather than waiting through a fixed forum interval.

sections.heading: Urgent symptoms versus a routine booking
paragraphs: Book a routine preconception review when a condition needs optimisation, a medicine needs discussion before conception, cycles are persistently irregular, you have had recurrent pregnancy loss, or a previous pregnancy had a significant complication.

Seek urgent local care now—not after conception—for chest pain, fainting, very heavy bleeding, acute severe pelvic pain, or sudden neurological symptoms. A planned pregnancy does not convert an emergency into a routine booking. If you conceive before the checklist is finished, contact your clinician promptly rather than stopping medicines alone.

faqs.question: Do I need folic acid if I already eat greens and dals?
faqs.answer: Food helps, but India's NHM and WHO still advise a daily 400 mcg folic acid supplement from preconception into early pregnancy for neural-tube defect prevention. Diet alone is hard to rely on for that specific goal; our folic acid guide explains timing and label checks.

faqs.question: Should my partner come to the preconception visit?
faqs.answer: When possible, yes. Partner medicines, smoking, alcohol, workplace exposures and any prior semen or fertility history can change next steps. Bring both histories so questions are not left half-answered at home.
